{{Short description|Curves whose limit does not preserve length}}

{{For|the drawing of an impossible staircase|Penrose stairs}}

[[File:Quadrat Diagonale.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|Staircases converging pointwise to the diagonal of a unit square, but not converging to its length]]
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''staircase paradox''' is a [[Pathological (mathematics)|pathological example]] showing that [[Limit (mathematics)|limits]] of curves do not necessarily preserve their [[length]].{{r|moscovich}}

==Description==
The paradox consists of a sequence of "staircase" [[polygonal chain]]s in a [[unit square]], formed from horizontal and vertical [[line segment]]s of decreasing length, so that these staircases [[uniform convergence|converge uniformly]] to the diagonal of the square.{{r|farrell}} However, each staircase has length two, while the length of the diagonal is the [[square root of 2]] (approximately 1.4142), so the sequence of staircase lengths does not converge to the length of the diagonal.{{r|sedaghat|stewart}}

[[Martin Gardner]] calls this "an ancient geometrical paradox".{{r|gardner}} The staircase paradox shows that, for curves under uniform convergence, the length of a curve is not a [[continuous function]] of the curve.{{r|sinila}}

==Explanation==
For any [[smooth curve]], polygonal chains with segment lengths decreasing to zero, connecting consecutive [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] along the curve, always converge to the [[arc length]]. The failure of the staircase curves to converge to the correct length can be explained by the fact that some of their vertices do not lie on the diagonal.{{r|krantz}}

==Usage==
[[File:circle_staircase_paradox.svg|thumb|upright|A fallacious approach to calculating the circumference of a circle due to the staircase paradox]]
As well as highlighting the need for careful definitions of arc length in mathematics education,{{r|bennett}} the staircase paradox has applications in [[digital geometry]], where it motivates methods of estimating the perimeter of pixelated shapes that do not merely sum the lengths of boundaries between pixels.{{r|kleyip}}

In [[higher dimension]]s, the [[Schwarz lantern]] provides an analogous example showing that polyhedral surfaces that [[pointwise convergence|converge pointwise]] to a curved surface do not necessarily converge to its area, even when the vertices all lie on the surface.{{r|ogilvy}}

==See also==
*[[Coastline paradox]], similar paradox where a straight segment approximation diverges
*[[Aliasing]], a more general phenomenon of inaccuracies caused by pixelation
*[[Cantor function|Cantor staircase]], a fractal curve along the diagonal of a unit square
*[[Taxicab geometry]], in which the lengths of the staircases and of the diagonal are equal
